## Hard Negative Cases

### SC-3: Off-By-One Mutations — NOT RESOLVED

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| n_changed | 39 |
| AUROC | 0.544 |
| Inversion delta | +0.083 (CHANGED scores higher than EQUIV) |
| CI | [0.484, 0.608] |
| Near-identical traces | 84.6% (similarity > 0.99) |
| Verdict | NOT_RESOLVED |

**Why SC-3 fails**: Off-by-one mutations (e.g., `<=` vs `<`, `n` vs `n-1`) cause minimal changes to execution traces with the V2 canonical inputs. 84.6% of changed programs produce near-identical dynamic genomes to their correct counterparts. The 8 canonical inputs do not specifically test boundary conditions for each program's off-by-one bug.

**Theoretical explanation**: Dynamic genome features are coarse-grained aggregate statistics. An off-by-one error typically produces at most 1 different trace out of 8 input runs (if that input happens to trigger the boundary). With n_runs=5 averaging, the single different trace is diluted.

### SC-11: Wrong-Variable Mutations — FULLY RESOLVED

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| n_changed | 39 |
| AUROC | 0.790 |
| Inversion delta | -0.227 (CHANGED scores LOWER than EQUIV — correct direction) |
| CI | [0.721, 0.845] |
| Near-identical traces | 17.9% |
| Verdict | FULLY_RESOLVED |

**Why SC-11 succeeds**: Wrong-variable mutations (substituting one variable for another in a computation) often cause different execution paths, exceptions, or coverage patterns across multiple canonical inputs. The dynamic genome captures these differences in `exception_rate`, `coverage_consistency`, and `anon_call_freq`.
